title: How did Vancouver move one hour away from Seattle?
text:
DERAILED / CLOCKS & COORDINATES / NOVEMBER 2026




Nothing moved on the map. But on November 1, 2026, the clocks on either side of the border stopped agreeing.

The two cities are as close as they were yesterday. British Columbia decided to keep most of its clocks on UTC−7, while Washington State still turns back to UTC−8 for winter. The result? Vancouver and Seattle no longer share the same winter time.


A clock is a surprisingly political object. Start with Vancouver and Seattle; switch the date and watch what changes.

 INTERACTIVE EXPLORATION 


  
    01The border
    02The West
    03Across Canada
  
  Two neighbouring cities. One hour of difference.
  
    
      CHOOSE A DATE
      
        Oct 31, 2026
        Nov 2, 2026
      
    
    
      VANCOUVER COMPARED WITH
      Seattle
    
  
  
    
      BRITISH COLUMBIA
      
      9:00 AM
      UTC−7
    
    =
    
      WASHINGTON
      
      9:00 AM
      UTC−7
    
  
  Loading clock comparison…
  
    
    Loading geographic data…
     Selected cities  Great-circle distance
  
  
    The physical distance doesn't change.
    GeoNames representative points. Turf.js computes great-circle distance; the line is illustrative, not a driving route or time-zone boundary.
  
  


Try it: Start with Seattle and flip the date. Then select The West, add San Francisco or Calgary, and finally select Across Canada to discover Newfoundland’s half-hour offset.




On October 31, Vancouver, Seattle and San Francisco are all at UTC−7. On November 2, Washington and California have fallen back to UTC−8 while Vancouver stays on UTC−7.
At 9:00 AM in Vancouver, the clock in Seattle reads 8:00 AM. The difference will disappear again when the U.S. starts daylight saving time in March 2027, assuming the rules stay the same.
And the travel distance? Exactly unchanged. The Washington State Department of Transportation notes that an approximately four-hour Amtrak journey can appear as three hours in one direction and five in the other when shown in local departure and arrival times.
Explore the Western cities ↑



Before 2026, Vancouver and Victoria moved their clocks twice a year. Fort St. John already stayed at UTC−7 all year. Southeastern BC communities historically followed Mountain Time arrangements.
Calgary is another twist: Alberta is also staying on UTC−6 year-round from November 2026. That keeps Calgary one hour ahead of Vancouver while Seattle moves one hour behind.
One provincial boundary never guaranteed one clock rule. And a place’s IANA time-zone ID does not, by itself, explain which local government made that rule.
Compare BC and Alberta ↑



Toronto still falls back, so its winter difference from Vancouver shrinks from three hours to two. And St. John’s, Newfoundland, follows a half-hour time zone: its winter UTC offset is −3:30 rather than a whole number of hours.
The map expands, but the governing idea remains small: a geographic distance is not a time difference.
Explore across Canada ↑



A point. GeoNames provides representative city coordinates and identifiers.
A name. GeoNames also supplies IANA identifiers such as America/Vancouver, America/Edmonton, and America/St_Johns. They encode time-zone histories, not a single permanent offset.
A rule on a date. Government decisions determine local time policies. The R + DuckDB preparation script joins the GeoNames places to explicitly documented UTC offsets for two instants and exports a small JSON file. JavaScript reads that file to update the clocks; Turf.js computes the distances.
This is deliberately a dated editorial snapshot, not a universal time-zone conversion service. The source definitions and the rules are kept separate.



The next time someone says two cities are “in the same time zone,” there’s a useful follow-up question:
On which date?


Sources & method. Place coordinates: GeoNames (CC BY 4.0). Clock policies: Government of BC, Government of Alberta, Washington State, NIST, and St. John’s 2026 clock-change history. Amtrak travel example: WSDOT. The comparison uses 16:00 UTC on October 31 and November 2, not live clocks. Selected city points are not time-zone polygons. Editorial issue · Research issue.

title: Sardine Lab — One fish, then a school
text:
DERAILED / MARINE LIFE / EXPERIMENT NO. 016




At Aquamarine Fukushima, a shimmering school of Japanese sardines moved as though it were a single creature. Nobody seemed to be in charge. What happens if we start with one fish, make a lot more, and give them a handful of rules?


GEOMETRY → MOVEMENT → NEIGHBOURS → EMERGENCE


  
    
      THE SARDINE LAB / 01—03
      
    
    No leader. Just neighbours.
  

  
    
    
      48 SARDINES
      48 FISH · AVG 0 PX/S
    
  

  
    
      
        01 / FISH GENERATOR
        Same species. Slightly different individuals.
      
      
        Number of fish 48
          
        
        Fish size 38%
          
        
        Body length 120
          
        
        Body depth 32
          
        
      
      
        ↝ New proportions
        ↻ New school
      
    

    
      
        02 / MOVEMENT ENGINE
        Each fish has its own heading and speed.
      
      
        Free swim
        Follow target
      
      Fish choose their own paths.
      
        Swim speed 1.1
          
        
        Turning agility 2.5
          
        
      
      
        ✳ New destination
        
          
          Trace one fish (not the leader)
        
      
    

    
      
        03 / SCHOOLING RULES
        What if each fish notices its neighbours?
      
      
        Independent
        Schooling
      
      Each fish notices only nearby neighbours.
      
        Three local rules
        
          Separation 1.4
            
          
          Alignment 1.0
            
          
          Cohesion 1.0
            
          
        
      
    
  

  
    Pause swimming
    Reset experiment
  
  Start with Independent. Then turn on Schooling without resetting the fish. Switch individual rules down to zero to see their contribution. The dotted amber path belongs to one observed fish, not a designated leader. Tap the tank to offer all fish the same destination.



The generator draws one recognizable sardine using Canvas paths: silver back, pale belly, forked tail, and an eye. We make an array of fish, each with a slightly different size, heading, and tail rhythm. The fish size slider makes them small enough to share the tank.
Each fish keeps its own movement state. Its direction of travel can change all the way around the tank, but we draw it from the side and mirror left to right, so its belly stays down.



Switch to Independent. Each fish wanders and steers away from the tank walls, but it does not know where the other sardines are. More fish alone doesn’t create a coordinated school.
Try raising the count, then dropping it to 1 to inspect the individual generator again. If you’d like a closer look, increase the fish size.



Turn on Schooling. Each sardine now responds only to nearby fish, using three ideas from the classic Boids simulation:

Separation: don’t crowd your closest neighbours.
Alignment: turn toward the direction nearby neighbours are moving.
Cohesion: steer toward the neighbourhood, not a central leader.

Try reducing alignment to zero. Do the fish still travel together? Try removing cohesion. Do they gradually drift apart? Raise separation and notice how tightly they can pack.
The simulation computes all the neighbour suggestions from the same moment, and only then updates the fish. That prevents the order of the array from accidentally giving some fish an informational advantage.



There is no invisible leader fish. Every swimmer runs the same local instructions. And the rules aren’t hard-coded fish formations: the patterns emerge from repeated interactions.
This is a playful, intentionally simplified computational model. Real sardines have sensory systems, predators, currents, and three-dimensional movement that our two-dimensional tank doesn’t attempt to reproduce.

If nobody is in charge, who decides where the school goes?


Inspired by a visit to Aquamarine Fukushima. DERAILED issue #16 · Gomasu story #115.
